noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand why simple, unicellular organisms can rely on diffusion for movement of substances in and out of the cell
understand the need for a transport system in multicellular organisms

primer.text: Why does an amoeba get by with a bare membrane while you need miles of vessels? Size is the answer. This note compares the surface-area-to-volume arithmetic of single cells against layered bodies, and shows what animals and plants built to beat the diffusion bottleneck.

lessons.title: Why Single Cells Need No Delivery Fleet
lessons.opening: A unicellular organism exchanges everything it needs directly across its membrane: its large surface relative to its volume keeps every interior point close to the outside, so diffusion, osmosis and active transport alone suffice.
keyPoints: Exchange happens by diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
Unicellular organisms have large surface areas relative to volume.
The distance from surface to centre stays short.
No specialised exchange surfaces are needed.
Amoeba manages its gas exchange across the cell membrane alone.

low.restatement: One small cell, big surface, short distances: plain diffusion keeps it alive.
low.analogy: A studio flat: every corner is within arm's reach of the window.
low.examPointer: Quote the ratio phrase — large surface area to volume ratio — verbatim.

medium.restatement: Because volume grows faster than surface as objects enlarge, a single cell's geometry guarantees short paths, so membrane transport meets every demand without internal plumbing.
medium.analogy: A small shop serves every shelf from one door; a warehouse needs aisles and forklifts.
medium.examPointer: Turn the reasoning around: if a cell were giant, diffusion alone would starve its core.

check.stem: How do unicellular organisms exchange substances with their environment?

options.text: Across the cell membrane by diffusion, osmosis and active transport
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
They have no vessels.
Amoeba feeds by phagocytosis, but exchange of gases is membrane-level.
Stomata belong to leaves.

check.stem: What geometric property lets a single cell rely on diffusion?

options.text: A large surface area relative to its volume
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: A small surface area to save energy
options.explanation: Small surface would slow exchange.

options.text: A spherical shape of maximum volume
options.explanation: Volume is the problem, not the goal.
Thick membranes lengthen diffusion paths.

check.stem: Why does an amoeba need no specialised exchange surface?

options.text: Its surface-to-centre distance is so short that membrane diffusion meets its needs
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
It exchanges constantly across the membrane.
Amoeba is not photosynthetic.

options.text: Because it lives out of water
options.explanation: Amoeba lives in water.

check.stem: Which direction does oxygen diffuse in an amoeba?

options.text: Inward, from the water where it is more concentrated
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
The cell consumes oxygen, so the gradient points in.
Consumption keeps the inward gradient.

options.text: It does not diffuse at all
options.explanation: Gas exchange runs by diffusion.

check.stem: Which transport methods does a single cell use for its exchanges?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Those are physical changes, not cell transport.
No organs exist to pump or filter.
That is a plant process.

check.stem: State why unicellular organisms can rely on diffusion alone.
check.modelAnswer: Their large surface area relative to volume keeps diffusion distances short, so membrane exchange meets all their needs.

check.stem: Name the organism used as the single-celled example here.
check.modelAnswer: The amoeba exchanges oxygen inward and carbon dioxide outward across its membrane.

check.stem: Explain why diffusion distance matters so much to a single cell.
check.modelAnswer: Because diffusion slows steeply with distance, and a short surface-to-centre path lets gases and wastes move fast enough to service the whole cell volume.

check.stem: A single-celled organism grows to ten times its diameter. Predict its exchange problem.
check.modelAnswer: Its volume rises far faster than its surface area, so the interior sits far from the membrane, and diffusion alone can no longer supply the core.

lessons.title: Why Multicellular Bodies Need Plumbing
lessons.opening: Multicellular bodies stack many cell layers deep, so diffusion alone is far too slow to reach the interior; animals answered with a circulatory system in blood, plants with a vascular system of xylem and phloem.
keyPoints: Many cell layers make the surface-to-centre distance too long.
Diffusion alone would be too slow to meet the body's needs.
The animal answer is the circulatory system carrying blood.
Blood hauls oxygen, glucose, carbon dioxide, water and urea.
The plant answer is xylem upward for water and minerals, phloem for sugars.

low.restatement: Big bodies need delivery networks: blood in animals, sap pipelines in plants.
low.analogy: A city needs courier vans once houses spread beyond walking distance.
low.examPointer: Name both systems and both plant vessels when comparing.

medium.restatement: Layered tissue multiplies the diffusion path beyond usefulness, so mass flow systems carry substances the whole way and exchange happens only at the endpoints.
medium.analogy: Motorways for the long haul, footpaths for the doorstep.
medium.examPointer: Use "too slow" plus the named systems; that pairing is the standard mark line.

check.stem: Why can multicellular organisms not rely on diffusion alone?

options.text: Their many cell layers make diffusion distances too long for adequate speed
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Because their skin blocks all diffusion
options.explanation: Skin is one layer; depth is the real issue.
Temperature is irrelevant to this argument.
Every cell has a membrane.

check.stem: Which system transports substances in animals?

options.text: The circulatory system, carrying them in the blood
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
That is the plant answer.
Lymph drains fluid; blood does the hauling.
Nerves carry signals, not substances.

check.stem: Which substances does animal blood typically carry?

options.text: Oxygen, glucose, carbon dioxide, water and urea
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Neither travels in blood.
Those belong to plants.
Antibodies ride along, but plaque is a deposit, not cargo.

check.stem: Which plant vessels move water upward from the roots?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Phloem distributes sugars and amino acids.
Stomata are leaf pores for gas exchange.
They absorb; xylem transports.

check.stem: What does the phloem distribute throughout the plant?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
That is the xylem's job.
Oxygen diffuses through air spaces.
Chlorophyll stays in the chloroplasts.

check.stem: State the transport systems of animals and plants.
check.modelAnswer: Animals use the circulatory system in the blood; plants use the vascular system of xylem and phloem.

check.stem: Name the two jobs of the plant vascular system.
check.modelAnswer: Xylem hauls water and minerals up from the roots, while phloem distributes sugars and amino acids.

check.stem: Explain why being many cells thick creates a transport need.
check.modelAnswer: Because each extra layer lengthens the diffusion path from the surface, and past a few layers the centre cannot be supplied quickly enough by diffusion alone.

check.stem: An flatworm is thin and flat; a roundworm is cylindrical. Which needs more transport provision and why?
check.modelAnswer: The cylindrical worm: its greater thickness puts interior cells farther from the surface, so diffusion alone struggles where the flatworm's short paths suffice.

glossary.definition: The net movement of particles down a concentration gradient.
The comparison that decides whether diffusion alone can service a body.
The animal transport network carried in the blood.
The plant transport network of xylem and phloem.
